Experiment_description: Baseline evaluation of LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct on the MultiJail multilingual safety benchmark across 10 languages, combined with a preliminary layer-wise semantic alignment analysis to identify a 'semantic bottleneck' layer for the proposed LASA (Language-Agnostic Semantic Alignment) method. Uses a rule-based refusal detector as ASR judge and computes cross-lingual hidden-state cosine similarity across layers of the transformer.
Significance: This establishes the baseline motivation for LASA by (a) quantifying the multilingual safety gap in a state-of-the-art aligned LLM and (b) empirically identifying an intermediate transformer layer where representations become most language-agnostic. Both findings are prerequisites for the proposed intervention: without a demonstrable ASR gap across resource levels there is no problem to solve, and without a semantic bottleneck layer there is no natural anchor point for cross-lingual safety alignment. The results support the LASA hypothesis and provide a concrete candidate intervention layer.
Description: The pipeline (1) loads LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct locally, (2) generates completions to MultiJail harmful prompts in 10 languages (en, it, zh, ko, ar, vi, th, bn, sw, jv), (3) applies a rule-based string-pattern refusal detector to compute ASR = 1 - refusal_rate, (4) aggregates ASR by language resource level (high/medium/low), (5) extracts hidden states across all 32 transformer layers for parallel prompts and computes pairwise cross-lingual cosine similarities to locate the layer with maximal semantic alignment (and via linear probing, minimal language-identity separability), and (6) produces visualizations of ASR and layer-wise alignment.

List_of_included_plots.description: Layer-wise language separability analysis showing linear probing accuracy for language identification across transformer layers (0-31) of LLaMA-3.1-8B. Accuracy starts ~0.72 at layer 0, peaks ~0.95-0.97 at layers 2-4, decreases through middle layers to a minimum ~0.75-0.78 at layers 14-16, and rises again at deeper layers. Red star marks the identified 'semantic bottleneck' layer.
List_of_included_plots.analysis: This is the strongest scientific finding of the node: an empirical, non-trivial U-shape in language-ID probing accuracy indicating that mid-network layers (~14-16) encode language-agnostic semantics. This directly supports the LASA hypothesis and provides a concrete target layer for downstream intervention. The pattern is consistent with prior interpretability findings that early layers encode surface/lexical language features while middle layers encode abstract semantics.

List_of_included_plots.description: Heatmap of cross-lingual cosine similarity of hidden states across languages at the bottleneck layer. Diagonal ~1.0; off-diagonal 0.60-0.85. Higher similarity clusters visible among linguistically related languages.
List_of_included_plots.analysis: Provides geometric evidence complementing the probing analysis: even where language identity is somewhat separable, semantic content is aligned across languages at the bottleneck layer. Clustering by linguistic family is a useful qualitative validation.

Key_numerical_results.description: Overall ASR (rule-based judge) across 10 languages on MultiJail for baseline LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct.
Key_numerical_results.analysis: A high aggregate ASR indicates the model, despite instruction tuning, exhibits substantial multilingual safety failures. Establishes headroom for the proposed LASA method.
Baseline safety alignment is relatively stronger for high-resource languages, consistent with training data distribution.
Intermediate safety degradation, showing a monotonic degradation trend with resource level.
Nearly double the ASR of high-resource languages, empirically confirming the multilingual safety gap motivating LASA.

Key_numerical_results.description: ASR for Bengali, Javanese, and Swahili individually.
Key_numerical_results.analysis: Complete safety failure in these low-resource languages under the rule-based judge — the model essentially never refuses harmful prompts, indicating alignment does not transfer to these languages.
Italian shows the strongest refusal behavior, an interesting outlier even among high-resource languages that may reflect training-set safety coverage.

Surprisingly high ASR for English suggests the rule-based judge may over-count attacks (false positives), which is a caveat for interpreting absolute numbers — but the relative resource-level ordering should still be informative.

Key_numerical_results.description: Maximum cross-lingual cosine similarity of hidden states at the best (bottleneck) layer.
Key_numerical_results.analysis: Near-perfect alignment of parallel-prompt representations at the identified layer, geometrically justifying the choice of bottleneck for language-agnostic anchoring.

Key_numerical_results.description: Minimum cross-lingual cosine similarity across layers.
Key_numerical_results.analysis: Large dynamic range in cross-lingual alignment across layers demonstrates that some layers are strongly language-specific while others are language-agnostic, validating the layer-selection approach.

Key_numerical_results.description: Mean cross-lingual cosine similarity across layers.
Key_numerical_results.analysis: High mean alignment suggests that language-agnostic semantics are broadly present in the model but concentrated most strongly at the identified bottleneck.
